subject: Agriculture
title: The Ogallala Aquifer
description: Learn The Ogallala Aquifer in one minute.

hook.text: The Ogallala Aquifer stretches under eight US states and waters 30% of America's irrigated cropland.

buildup.text: It holds water deposited by ancient rivers over millions of years—fossil water, almost irreplaceable.

discovery.text: Since the 1950s, pumping has dropped the water table by over 150 feet in some areas of west Texas.

twist.text: The aquifer recharges at about one inch per year. Farmers pump out feet. The math doesn't work.

climax.text: Parts of the southern Ogallala may be functionally depleted by 2050. No backup water source exists.

punchline.text: America's breadbasket runs on borrowed water—with no way to pay it back.

quiz.question: Why is the Ogallala Aquifer considered nearly irreplaceable?
options: It holds ancient 'fossil water' that recharges far slower than it's pumped

details.summary: The Ogallala Aquifer is one of the world's largest underground water reserves, underlying eight US states and irrigating one of America's most productive agricultural regions. This topic covers its geology, the depletion crisis, and what happens if it runs dry.
details.whyItMatters: The Ogallala irrigates about 27% of US farmland but is being pumped many times faster than it recharges. Its depletion would devastate US agriculture and global food markets.
takeaways: The Ogallala Aquifer underlies 174,000 square miles across eight US Great Plains states
It provides 30% of all US irrigation water for crops and 80% of drinking water in the region
Parts of the aquifer will be effectively depleted within 25 years at current pumping rates

faq.question: Why is the Ogallala Aquifer so important for US agriculture?
faq.answer: The Ogallala irrigates about 13 million acres of cropland across the Great Plains, producing a significant share of US wheat, corn, cotton, and beef. Without it, much of this land would revert to dryland farming with far lower yields.

faq.question: Can the Ogallala Aquifer be replenished?
faq.answer: Natural recharge is extremely slow—only about half an inch per year in most areas because the aquifer sits beneath thick impermeable clay layers. At current pumping rates, some sections would take thousands of years to refill naturally.
